title: Lecture #19: Java Nested Classes
topics: Use cases of static nested classes

questions.question: In `main`, you already have `Outer outer = new Outer();`. `Inner` is a non-static inner class of `Outer`. Which statement correctly creates an `Inner` object?
options: `Outer.Inner inner = new Outer.Inner();`
`Outer.Inner inner = outer.new Inner();`
`Outer.Inner inner = new Inner();`
`Outer.Inner inner = new Inner(outer);`
questions.explanation: An inner class object must be tied to a specific Outer object, so it is created with the `outerRef.new Inner()` syntax (or `new Outer().new Inner()`). `new Outer.Inner()` is how you create a static nested class; for an inner class it fails because no enclosing Outer instance is supplied.

questions.question: A static nested class `Inner` is declared inside `Outer`, which has a `private static int x` and an instance field `int y`. According to the lecture, how can code inside `Inner` read `y`?
options: Directly as `y`, because a nested class can see every member of its outer class
As `Outer.this.y`, because every nested class keeps a hidden reference to the outer object
Only through a reference to an `Outer` object, such as `outer.y`
It cannot read `y` at all, because `y` is not static
questions.explanation: A static nested class is not tied to any Outer instance, so it can directly use only Outer's static members (like `x`, even though it is private). To reach an instance member such as `y` it needs an explicit Outer reference, which is exactly what `Demo.java` does with its `Outer outer` field and `outer.y`. `Outer.this` only exists inside inner (non-static) classes.

questions.topic: Use cases of static nested classes
questions.question: In `BankAccount`, the interest formula lives in a `private static class InterestCalculator` with a static method `calculateYearly(...)`. A teammate asks why it isn't simply a separate top-level class. What is the best justification?
options: It is a helper used only by `BankAccount`, so nesting it as private groups it logically and hides it from the rest of the code
Static nested classes run faster than top-level classes because they are loaded together with the outer class
Only nested classes are allowed to declare static methods, so a top-level class could not hold `calculateYearly`
Making it private and static lets it read the instance fields of every `BankAccount` without a reference
questions.explanation: The lecture lists "helper class for an outer class" as a main use case: nesting gives logical grouping and the `private` modifier hides the helper from outside code. Top-level classes can of course have static methods, and a static nested class still cannot touch instance fields without an object reference.
questions.source: code: Demo.java (BankAccount, use-case comment); notes p1

questions.question: What happens when this code (from the lecture) is compiled and run?
options: It prints `6`
It prints `5`, because the local class captured `y` before the increment
It does not compile, because `y` is used inside the local class but is not effectively final
It compiles but throws an exception when `sayHello()` runs
questions.explanation: A local class may only use local variables of the enclosing method that are final or effectively final. `y++` reassigns `y`, so `y` is no longer effectively final and the compiler reports an error at `System.out.println(y)`. Nothing is printed, because the program never compiles.

questions.question: What is printed?
questions.explanation: Inside `show`, the plain name `x` means the closest declaration, the parameter (30). `this.x` is the Inner object's own field (20), and `Outer.this.x` reaches the field of the enclosing Outer object (10). Picking `30 30 10` assumes `this.x` also sees the parameter, but `this.x` always means a field.

questions.question: This is the lecture's anonymous-class example with one extra line added at the end of `main`. What is the result?
options: It prints `Hello`, `Hi, I am Aditya`, then `Hello`
It does not compile: `greet()` cannot be called through a `Person` reference
It prints `Hi, I am a person` and then `Hello`
It compiles, but `p2.greet()` throws an exception at runtime
questions.explanation: The anonymous class may add its own field and methods, but `p2` is declared as `Person`, and the compiler only lets you call methods that `Person` declares. `Person` has no `greet()`, so `p2.greet()` is a compile error, while `p2.introduce()` alone would print `Hello` and `Hi, I am Aditya`. Extra methods of an anonymous class can only be used from inside its own body.

questions.question: You are writing an `ApiClient` class and want to group its `Request` and `Response` DTOs inside it. Callers must be able to build a `Request` on its own, without first creating an `ApiClient`. Which declaration fits?
options: `public static class Request { ... }` inside `ApiClient`
`public class Request { ... }` (non-static inner class) inside `ApiClient`
A local class `Request` declared inside an `ApiClient` method
An anonymous subclass of `Object` assigned to a field in `ApiClient`
questions.explanation: A static nested class needs no instance of the outer class and can be created like a normal class (`new ApiClient.Request()`), which is why the lecture lists Request/Response DTOs and the Builder pattern as its use cases. A non-static inner class would force callers to write `client.new Request()`, and local or anonymous classes cannot be named from outside the method at all.

questions.question: A `Report` object holds a 50 MB array and has a non-static inner class `Row`. A long-lived cache stores only `Row` objects; the `Report` objects are no longer referenced anywhere else. Memory keeps growing. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: `Row` objects are stored on the stack, so they are never collected; move them to the heap with `new`
The cache must call `System.gc()` after storing rows; the inner class itself is not the issue
Inner classes cannot be garbage-collected until the JVM exits; convert `Row` into a local class
Each `Row` keeps a hidden reference to its `Report`, keeping every array alive; make `Row` a static nested class
questions.explanation: Every inner class object stores an implicit reference to the outer object that created it (the arrow from Inner to Outer in the lecture's heap diagram). While the cache holds a `Row`, its `Report` and its large array stay reachable. A static nested class has no such link, so the reports can be collected; calling `System.gc()` does not help because the reports are still reachable.
questions.source: notes p2-p3 (heap diagrams of Outer/Inner objects)

questions.question: The lecture notes say an inner class cannot have static members, yet `Demo2.java` declares `static int x` and `static void fun2()` inside a non-static inner class and calls `Outer.Inner.fun2()`. On Java 17, what is accurate?
options: The code does not compile on any Java version; only `static final` constants are ever allowed in inner classes
It compiles only because `fun2()` never uses an Outer instance; `static int x` alone would be an error
It compiles: since Java 16 inner classes may declare static members; before that only compile-time constant fields were allowed
It compiles, but each Outer object gets its own copy of `Inner.x`
questions.explanation: Before Java 16, an inner class could only declare static fields that were compile-time constants (`static final` with a constant value), which is the rule the notes describe. Java 16 (the records JEP) lifted this restriction, so on Java 17 the static field and static method compile. A static field still belongs to the class `Outer.Inner`, so there is one copy shared by all objects, not one per Outer object.

questions.question: In the notes, `greet()` declares `int y = 10`, defines a local class that prints `y`, and returns the local object. Later, after `greet()` has returned, the object's method still prints `10`. Why does Java require `y` to be effectively final for this to be allowed?
options: Because local variables are stored in the heap, and only final heap variables can be shared between objects
Because the local object can outlive the method's stack frame, so it keeps its own copy of `y`; that copy is only safe if `y` never changes
Because local classes are static, and static code may only read final variables
Because `y` is moved into the class's constant pool when the method finishes, and only final values fit there
questions.explanation: Local variables live in the method's stack frame, which disappears when `greet()` returns, but the local class object lives on the heap and may be used later. The compiler therefore copies the value of `y` into the object (the `y = 10` box inside the heap object in the notes). If `y` could change afterwards, the copy and the original would disagree, so Java only allows capture of final or effectively final variables.
